findings.summary: TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. pleaded guilty to conspiring to fail to maintain an anti-money laundering program and to launder money, resulting in a combined $1.8 billion penalty, including a $1.3 billion civil money penalty from FinCEN, a $450 million civil money penalty from the OCC, and a $543 million payment to the DOJ. The bank admitted to systemic BSA/AML failures, including excluding 92% of transaction volume from monitoring, enabling money laundering networks, and failing to report suspicious activity.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered TD Bank, N.A. to pay $27.76 million in total penalties, including $7.76 million in redress to affected consumers and a $20 million civil money penalty, for violating the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Regulation V by repeatedly furnishing inaccurate consumer credit information and failing to timely investigate disputes.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission ordered TD Bank to pay a $75 million civil monetary penalty for recordkeeping and supervision failures related to the firm-wide use of unapproved communication methods, admitting to violations of CFTC recordkeeping and supervision requirements.

TD Bank pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering in October 2024, resulting in a $3.09 billion settlement with U.S. regulators, including a $3.1 billion penalty and business restrictions. This led to multiple shareholder class actions alleging misrepresentations about AML controls, with one case surviving dismissal in October 2026 and proceeding to discovery.

A class action lawsuit alleging TD Bank failed to refund overdraft fees on accounts brought back to positive balance within its grace period was filed on October 2, 2025, and is listed as terminated in May 2026. The case was part of a series of overdraft fee disputes, including the Burns settlement ($32.2 million paid in 2025) and MDL 2613 ($70 million paid in 2020).

An Ontario Superior Court certified a class action on April 10, 2026, alleging TD Bank failed to pay vacation and holiday pay to commissioned Mobile Mortgage Specialists, in violation of the Canada Labour Code. TD Bank appealed the certification decision in May 2026.

A U.S. securities class action, Tiessen v. TD Bank, was filed in October 2024 and is ongoing. It alleges TD Bank and its executives made materially misleading statements about the effectiveness of its anti-money laundering controls between December 2021 and October 2024, leading to a drop in share price after the $3.09 billion AML settlement was disclosed. The court denied the motion to dismiss in October 2026, allowing the case to proceed to discovery.

On October 10, 2024, TD Bank N.A. and its parent company, TD Bank US Holding Company, pleaded guilty to conspiring to fail to maintain an anti-money laundering (AML) program compliant with the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), failing to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports (CTRs), and laundering monetary instruments. The failure to monitor transactions enabled three money laundering networks to move over $670 million through TD Bank accounts between 2019 and 2023. As part of the plea agreement, TD Bank will pay $1.8 billion in penalties, enhance its AML compliance program, and retain an independent monitor. The DOJ described this as the largest penalty ever imposed under the BSA and the first time a national bank has pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder money.

Wilfredo Aquino, a former TD Bank assistant store manager, pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and in October 2026 to accepting bribes as a bank employee. Between 2019 and February 2021, Aquino facilitated the movement of approximately $474 million through TD Bank accounts by accepting bribes, including over $11,000 in retail gift cards. From April 2022 to November 2023, he also facilitated the laundering of $4.8 million to Colombia by opening fraudulent accounts, issuing debit cards, and unblocking restricted cards.

Leonardo Ayala, a former TD Bank retail banker, pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and accepting bribes as a bank employee. From June to November 2023, Ayala facilitated the laundering of approximately $5.5 million to Colombia by opening fraudulent accounts, issuing over 150 debit cards to shell companies, and unblocking restricted cards. He received over $6,000 in bribes in cash and via digital payment networks.

Nunez, a former TD Bank employee, pleaded guilty in January 2026 to accepting bribes and facilitating a money laundering scheme that moved over $26 million from the U.S. to Colombia between March 2021 and October 2023. He opened dozens of accounts in shell company names, issued over 600 debit cards, and shipped cards to co-conspirators in Colombia, enabling over 120,000 ATM withdrawals.

TD Bank N.A. pleaded guilty on October 10, 2024, to conspiring to fail to maintain an anti-money laundering program compliant with the Bank Secrecy Act, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments. The bank’s failures enabled three money laundering networks, including one assisted by five TD Bank employees, to transfer over $670 million between 2019 and 2023. As part of the resolution, TD Bank agreed to pay $1.8 billion in penalties, including a $1.4 billion criminal fine, and will be subject to a four-year independent monitor.

On October 10, 2024, FinCEN assessed a record $1.3 billion civil penalty against TD Bank for willfully failing to file Suspicious Activity Reports on thousands of suspicious transactions totaling approximately $1.5 billion, and for delaying or misleading Currency Transaction Reports. The violations enabled illicit activity including fentanyl trafficking, terrorist financing, and human trafficking, with trillions of dollars in transactions going unmonitored.

On December 23, 2021, TD Bank, N.A. settled with OFAC for $115,005.04 related to apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. The violations included processing 1,479 transactions totaling $382,685.38 for employees of the North Korean mission to the United Nations without a license and maintaining accounts for a U.S. resident listed on the SDN List, resulting in 145 apparent violations.

TD Bank, N.A. confirmed a data breach between January 7 and January 30, 2026, caused by an insider threat involving a bank employee who accessed and misused customer data, including names, Social Security numbers, account numbers, and transactional data. The breach was reported on June 15, 2026, and TD Bank is conducting an internal investigation, notifying affected customers, and enhancing its data protection protocols.

TD Bank, N.A. reported a data breach on August 27, 2026, involving one of its employees compromising customer personal information, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, account numbers, and transactional data. The incident affected two New Hampshire residents, and TD Bank notified them in writing, offering two years of free credit monitoring through a Fraud-Defender membership.

TD Bank, N.A. experienced a data breach between December 22, 2025, and March 11, 2026, when an employee accessed and misused customer account information, including names, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and transactional data. TD Bank began notifying affected customers on May 26, 2026, and the incident is under investigation by the bank's corporate security team.

TD Bank, N.A. was involved in a data breach incident in 2023 and another in 2024, both involving employees improperly accessing customer data, leading to multiple class action lawsuits, including Crumpe v. TD Bank N.A., which alleges systemic failures in data security and violations of consumer protection laws.

TD Bank was ordered by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to pay $28 million in 2024 for repeatedly providing inaccurate and fraudulent information to consumer reporting agencies, including data on bankruptcies and delinquencies, and failing to properly investigate disputes for over a year. The CFPB found systemic failures in TD Bank's management and governance, with leadership prioritizing growth over compliance.

In 2025, TD Bank reduced the total direct compensation of CEO Bharat Masrani by 89% for 2024, from $13.3 million to $1.5 million, and cut variable compensation by at least 25% for the rest of the Senior Executive Team due to the bank's significant Anti-Money Laundering (AML) failures. This executive accountability action was tied to governance failures and the impact on the U.S. retail business.

In 2025, TD Bank implemented a $30 million reduction in variable compensation for 41 executives, including those no longer with the bank, due to leadership responsibility for AML failures and governance shortcomings, further reflecting executive accountability for systemic compliance failures.
